title: Exploring elementary pre-service teachers’ instrumental genesis in designing AI chatbots
venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary pre-service teachers design AI chatbots for mathematics instruction and how their design decisions reveal instrumental genesis, meaning the reciprocal shaping between the designer and the digital artifact. The study asks what instructional functions teachers assign to chatbots, what design considerations they embed in prompts, and what constraints or failures they encounter when trying to make the chatbot behave as intended.

The intervention was a four-week chatbot-design project embedded in an advanced mathematics education course at a South Korean university of education. Eleven elementary pre-service teachers first received a lecture on generative AI and prompt engineering techniques, then used the Wrtn generative AI platform with GPT-4 to build chatbots for grade 5–6 number-and-operations content. They submitted lesson plans, prompts, chatbot links, and reflective reports; the analysis focused on the initial design artifacts and reflections.

Findings show that teachers designed chatbots for four main instructional functions: problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual understanding, and real-life application. Their prompts commonly incorporated scaffolding, affective support, bounded autonomy tied to the curriculum, and gamification. The study concludes that pre-service teachers can move beyond simple tool use to deliberate instructional design with AI, but they often struggle with curriculum non-compliance, limited diversity in chatbot outputs, incomplete scaffolding, and unpredictable responses outside the prompt scope. The author argues that teacher education should emphasize reflective prompt design, curriculum alignment, and adaptive mediation of AI tools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with thematic analysis of 11 pre-service teachers’ chatbot designs and reflections. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not test learning outcomes or use a causal design, so it meets limited credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful instructional design implications for AI-supported mathematics learning, but it reports no student outcome effects and no classroom implementation results. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service teachers designed ChatGPT-like generative AI chatbots in Wrtn for elementary mathematics instruction in the number and operations domain, using prompt engineering to make the chatbot act as a problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual-understanding, or application-support instrument.
Gamified chatbot lesson designs with storylines, target scores, secret codes, and level-based challenges to motivate elementary students while solving arithmetic tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The study qualitatively found that pre-service teachers designed chatbots to support mathematical numeracy through problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual understanding, and real-life application. However, the paper did not evaluate student learning gains; it instead documents intended instructional functions and design constraints in 11 chatbot designs, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of chatbot prompts and reflective reports for intended mathematics-learning functions

finding.finding_summary: Participants intentionally built affective support into most chatbot designs, aiming to increase student motivation through friendly, polite, and encouraging responses. The study reports these as design intentions only and does not measure student engagement or motivation outcomes, so no quantitative effect estimate is available.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of prompts for affective support and gamification features

finding.finding_summary: The chatbots were deliberately designed to promote scaffolding, bounded autonomy, and learning-by-teaching, all of which are intended to support metacognitive and critical-thinking processes. The paper provides qualitative evidence of these intended mechanisms but no direct assessment of durable-skill outcomes in students.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of prompt design and reflective reports for scaffolding, bounded autonomy, and learning-by-teaching mechanisms
